etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hoke, from Old English hōc, from Proto-West Germanic *hōk, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz, variant of *hakô (“hook”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kog-, *keg-, *keng- (“peg, hook, claw”).

definitions.definition: A rod bent into a curved shape, typically with one end free and the other end secured to a rope or other attachment.
A barbed metal hook used for fishing; a fishhook.
Any of various hook-shaped agricultural implements such as a billhook.

quote.citation: 1819 September 19, John Keats, “To Autumn”, in Lamia, Isabella, the Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems, London:  […]  [Thomas Davison] for Taylor and Hessey, […], published 1820, →OCLC, stanza 2, page 138:
quote.text: Or on a half-reap'd furrow sound asleep, / Drowsed with the fume of poppies, while thy hook  / Spares the next swath and all its twinèd flowers: [...]

definitions.definition: The curved needle used in the art of crochet.
The part of a hinge which is fixed to a post, and on which a door or gate hangs and turns.
A loop shaped like a hook under certain written letters, for example, g and j.
A tie-in to a current event or trend that makes a news story or editorial relevant and timely.
A snare; a trap.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:
quote.text: A shop of all the qualities, that manLoues woman for, besides that hooke of Wiuing,

definitions.definition: An advantageous hold.

quote.citation: 2020, Joel W. Barrows, Deep Red Cover:
quote.text: “What makes you so sure that nobody knows you've got a hook into him?” Ward asked.

definitions.definition: (in the plural) The projecting points of the thighbones of cattle; called also hook bones.
(informal) Removal or expulsion from a group or activity.
(agriculture) A field sown two years in succession.
(authorship) A brief, punchy opening statement intended to get attention from an audience, reader, or viewer, and make them want to continue to listen to a speech, read a book, or watch a play.
(narratology) A gimmick or element of a creative work intended to be attention-grabbing for the audience; a compelling idea for a story that will be sure to attract people's attention.

quote.citation: 2019 August 14, A. A. Dowd, “Good Boys Puts a Tween Spin on the R-rated Teen Comedy, to Mostly Funny Effect”, in The A.V. Club‎[1], archived from the original on 4 March 2021:
quote.text: The hook of Good Boys, Hollywood's latest odyssey of comic adolescent mischief, is that the kids behaving badly are, for once, truly kids.

definitions.definition: (bridge, slang) A finesse.
(card games, slang) A jack (the playing card).
(geography) A spit or narrow cape of sand or gravel turned landward at the outer end, such as Sandy Hook in New Jersey.
(music) A catchy musical phrase which forms the basis of a popular song.

quote.citation: 2017 January 20, Annie Zaleski, “AFI sounds refreshed and rejuvenated on its 10th album, AFI (The Blood Album)”, in The A.V. Club‎[2]:
quote.text: Guitarist Jade Puget and vocalist Davey Havok have distilled AFI’s strengths (a ferocious, post-hardcore rhythmic backbone; goth-tinctured, post-punky guitars; and Havok’s desperate, dramatic croon) into 14 taut, hook-driven songs.

definitions.definition: (nautical, informal) A ship's anchor.
(programming) Part of a system's operation that can be intercepted to change or augment its behaviour.

quote.citation: 2015, Rachel Alt-Simmons, Agile by Design, page 182:
quote.text: In lieu of those unneeded hooks, write code to fail fast and prevent gaps from becoming a problem.

definitions.definition: (Scrabble) An instance of playing a word perpendicular to a word already on the board, adding a letter to the start or the end of the word to form a new word.

quote.citation: 2003, Andrew Fisher, David Webb, The Art of Scrabble‎[3], →ISBN, page 58:
quote.text: Setup plays can also be made when you do not have the needed letter but believe your opponent doesn't know the hook owing to its obscurity.

definitions.definition: (typography) A diacritical mark shaped like the upper part of a question mark, as in ỏ.
(typography, rare) A háček.

quote.citation: 2003, Language Issues, XV-XVIII, page 36:
quote.text: Common diacritics in Slavonic language are the hook ˇ (as in haček – Czech for ‘hook’) and the stroke ´ (robić – Polish for ‘do/make’).

quote.citation: 2003, David Adams, The Song and Duet Texts of Antonín Dvořák, page 168:
quote.text: In Czech, palatalization is normally indicated by the symbol ˇ, called haček or “hook.”

quote.citation: 2004, Keesing’s Record of World Events L:i–xii, page unknown
quote.text: In detailing the proposed shortening of the Czech Republic to Česko…the hook (hacek) erroneously appeared over the letter “e” instead of the “C”.

definitions.definition: (baseball) A curveball.

(basketball) a basketball shot in which the offensive player, usually turned perpendicular to the basket, gently throws the ball with a sweeping motion of his arm in an upward arc with a follow-through which ends over his head. Also called hook shot.
(bowling) A ball that is rolled in a curved line.

quote.citation: 1969, Harold Keith, Sports and Games‎[4], page 102:
quote.text: However, for pins on the bowler's right, such as the 3, 6, 9, or 10, move more toward the center of the foul line if you bowl a straight ball or slightly to the left of the center of the foul line if you bowl a hook.

definitions.definition: (boxing) a type of punch delivered with the arm rigid and partially bent and the fist travelling nearly horizontally mesially along an arc

quote.citation: 2011 December 18, Ben Dirs, “Carl Froch outclassed by dazzling Andre Ward”, in BBC Sport‎[5]:
quote.text: American Ward was too quick and too slick for his British rival, landing at will with razor sharp jabs and hooks and even bullying Froch at times.

definitions.definition: (cricket) A type of shot played by swinging the bat in a horizontal arc, hitting the ball high in the air to the leg side, often played to balls which bounce around head height.
(golf) A golf shot that (for the right-handed player) curves unintentionally to the left. (See draw, slice, fade.)
The amount of spin placed on a bowling ball.
Senses relating to sports.
(Canada, Australia, military) Any of the chevrons denoting rank.
(slang) A prostitute.

quote.citation: 1983, G. W. Levi Kamel, Downtown Street Hustlers, page 160:
quote.text: I was talkin' to a couple of the 'hooks' (female prostitutes) I know.

definitions.definition: (UK, slang, obsolete) A pickpocket.

quote.citation: 1885, Michael Davitt, Leaves from a Prison Diary, page 18:
quote.text: He preceded me to Dartmoor, where I found his fame even more loudly trumpeted than ever, especially by Manchester “hooks” (pickpockets), who boast of being the rivals of the “Cocks,” or Londoners, in the art of obtaining other people's property without paying for it.

quote.citation: 2003, David W. Maurer, Whiz Mob: A Correlation of the Technical Argot of Pickpockets with Their Behavior Pattern, page 58:
quote.text: "Everybody's a tool over there. Everybody's a hook, except them four guys on the points of the compass. They are eight or ten strong over there." But all professional pickpockets, however expert or however clumsy, operate on the basis of the situation just outlined.

definitions.definition: (surfing) Synonym of shoulder (“the part of a wave that has not yet broken”)

quote.citation: 1963, Grant W. Kuhns, On Surfing, page 67:
quote.text: This maneuver involves a sharp turn, back into the hook of the wave.

definitions.definition: (nautical, chiefly historical) A knee-shaped wooden join connecting the keel to the stem (post forming the frontmost part of the bow) or the sternpost in cog-like vessels or similar vessels.
(transitive) To attach a hook to.
(intransitive) To become attached, as by a hook.
(transitive) To catch with a hook (hook a fish).
(transitive) To work yarn into a fabric using a hook; to crochet.

quote.citation: 1917, L M Montgomery, Anne's House of Dreams:
quote.text: No one seems to want anything but hooked mats now.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To insert in a curved way reminiscent of a hook.
(transitive) To ensnare or obligate someone, as if with a hook.
(UK, US, slang, archaic) To steal.
(transitive) To connect (hook into, hook together).
(usually in passive) To make addicted; to captivate.
(cricket, golf, basketball) To play a hook shot.

quote.citation: 2012, Roland Johnson, Jeremya Jones: A King's Kid, page 93:
quote.text: "Hey, Sara! Watch this hook shot!" he shouted as he hooked the ball right through the net—swish!

definitions.definition: (rugby) To succeed in heeling the ball back out of a scrum (used particularly of the team's designated hooker).
(field hockey, ice hockey) To engage in the illegal maneuver of hooking (i.e., using the hockey stick to trip or block another player)
(soccer, bowling) To swerve a ball; kick or throw a ball so it swerves or bends.

quote.citation: 2010 December 29, Sam Sheringham, “Liverpool 0 - 1 Wolverhampton”, in BBC‎[6]:
quote.text: The Reds carved the first opening of the second period as Glen Johnson's pull-back found David Ngog but the Frenchman hooked wide from six yards.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, slang) To engage in prostitution.
(Scrabble) To play a word perpendicular to another word by adding a single letter to the existing word.
(bridge, slang) To finesse.
(transitive) To seize or pierce with the points of the horns, as cattle in attacking enemies; to gore.
(intransitive) To bend; to be curved.

quote.citation: 2020, Roman Martin, Azores: The finest coastal and mountain walks, page 229:
quote.text: 10 mins later, at the point where the road hooks sharp to the left, continue straight on through the wood along a mule track  […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move or go with a sudden turn.

pronunciation: sometimes in Northern England and Ireland, otherwise obsolete
